title: The Rise of Humanoid Robots in 2026

slides.heading: The Rise of Humanoid Robots
slides.body: How machines that look and move like us are reshaping factories, homes, and the future of work

slides.heading: Why Now?
slides.body: Breakthroughs in AI, motor control, and battery technology have converged in 2025–2026. Robots that once stumbled on stairs can now fold laundry, sort packages, and assist surgeons — at a cost falling faster than anyone predicted.

slides.heading: The Big Players
slides.body: Tesla's Optimus, Figure AI's Figure-02, Boston Dynamics' Atlas, and Agility Robotics' Digit are in a race to deploy at scale. Chinese manufacturers like Unitree and UBTECH are also shipping thousands of units to factories across Asia.

slides.heading: Factory Floors First
slides.body: Automotive and logistics warehouses are the first major adopters. BMW, Mercedes, and Amazon run pilot programs where humanoid robots handle repetitive tasks alongside human workers — operating on three shifts without fatigue or breaks.

slides.heading: Learning by Watching
slides.body: Modern humanoid robots learn new tasks through imitation — a human demonstrates a motion once or twice, and the robot replicates and generalizes it. This "teleoperation + diffusion model" approach cuts programming time from weeks to hours.

slides.heading: Cost Curve Is Falling Fast
slides.body: In 2022 a capable humanoid prototype cost over $1 million. By 2026 production units are being quoted at $30,000–$70,000 — comparable to a compact car. Analysts project sub-$20,000 models before 2030 as supply chains mature.

slides.heading: Safety & Regulation
slides.body: The EU AI Act now classifies unsupervised humanoid robots as "high-risk" AI systems, requiring certification before deployment in public spaces. The US is still drafting federal guidelines, leaving a patchwork of state-level rules in place.

slides.heading: Jobs: Threat or Opportunity?
slides.body: The IMF estimates humanoid robots could automate 15–20% of physical labor roles by 2035. Economists are divided: optimists point to past automation waves that created new job categories; pessimists warn the pace this time may outstrip retraining capacity.

slides.heading: Coming to Homes & Hospitals
slides.body: Elder care and hospital assistance are the next frontier. Japan — facing a critical nursing shortage — has fast-tracked approval for robot assistants in care homes. Early trials show robots can safely lift patients, deliver medication, and monitor vital signs.

slides.heading: The Robot Era Has Begun
slides.body: Humanoid robots are no longer science fiction — they're clocking shifts in real factories today. Whether they become partners or disruptors depends on the policies, investments, and conversations we start right now.
